title: Where authority comes from
hook: Protestants say scripture alone is the final authority; Catholics and Orthodox read scripture within the church's living tradition

segments.voice: Yesterday, theology: words about God. Your line was words fall short, and help. What was the one sentence you wrote? Day one thousand sixty-three.

Paul and Silas slip out of one Greek city by night and arrive in a town called Berea. They go to the synagogue and Paul speaks. The listeners don't simply nod along, and they don't throw him out either. They open the scriptures, and keep checking, day after day, whether what he said holds up. The book of Acts admires them for it: "These were more noble than those in Thessalonica." Which raises a question that would one day divide churches. When a teacher and a text seem to disagree, who has the final word? Today's word: sola scriptura.

Sola scriptura is Latin for scripture alone. It became a watchword of the Protestant Reformation. Luther and other Reformers said the Bible is the final authority, over every teacher, council and pope. Tradition can be good and useful, they said, but scripture is the judge of it. And they pointed to Berea: the people there "searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so," even with an apostle in the room. Catholics and Orthodox Christians see it another way. For them, scripture and the church's living tradition belong together. The New Testament was written inside the church, and the whole Bible was read aloud in its worship and handed on with its teaching, so it is read within that tradition, not apart from it. Catholics speak of the church's teaching office guarding the faith; the Orthodox speak of the councils, the early fathers and the mind of the church. They point to Paul: "stand fast, and hold the traditions which ye have been taught, whether by word, or our epistle." By word, or by letter. Both. And each side has its reply. Protestants say the apostles' teaching is now found in their writings, so scripture is where you check it. Catholics and Orthodox ask who decides what scripture means when sincere readers disagree. Protestants add that scripture alone was never meant to be scripture with no history: Lutheran and Anglican churches, among others, still say the old creeds, because they hold that the creeds agree with the Bible. Underneath the argument is a question that turns up in ordinary life too. When good voices disagree, whose do you trust, and why?

Here's the practice: notice who you trust, and why. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one question that matters to you. What's right, what's true, what to do next. Now notice where you go first for an answer. A book. A pastor. A parent. A friend. Your own gut. Just notice it, without grading it. Then ask, gently, why that voice. Because it has been right before? Because it loves you? Because it was simply there first? If you pray, you can bring the question to God as well. The bell holds the time.
Sola scriptura. Latin for scripture alone: the Protestant teaching that the Bible is the final authority over every other voice.
Your line: where do you stand? Today, when someone tells you something is true, notice for a second what you check it against. Day one thousand sixty-three.

howItsDone: Protestant churches teach that scripture is the final authority, often while still saying the ancient creeds; Catholic and Orthodox churches read scripture together with the church's tradition, councils and teachers.

myth: sola scriptura means ignoring all history and creeds
Lutheran and Anglican churches, among others, still say the old creeds, holding that they agree with the Bible.
Catholics and Orthodox read scripture within the church's tradition
for them, scripture and tradition belong together, handed on in the church.
Acts criticizes the Bereans for doubting Paul
Acts admires them: "these were more noble than those in Thessalonica."

fork.setup: you're in the synagogue at Berea, and a traveling teacher named Paul has just said something new about the scriptures. what do you do?
options: accept every word, since he's clearly sincere.
go home and search the scriptures, day after day.
drive him out of town before he causes trouble.
fork.reveal: the Bereans "searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so," and Acts calls them noble for it. Protestants and Catholics alike can admire that care, and still read it differently.

original.note: Latin: scripture alone, a watchword of the Reformation.

trapdoor: what you thought: Protestants read the Bible and Catholics don't.
what it means: everyone reads it. the argument is about where final authority sits, in scripture alone, or in scripture with the church's tradition.
what a scholar hears: both sides quote scripture for their view. the Bereans checked an apostle against the scriptures; Paul tells the Thessalonians to hold traditions by word or by letter.

notes: Audit (fresh reviewer): all KJV/BCP quotations checked word for word, attributions and framing checked; no change needed.
Hook follows Acts 17:10–12 (Paul and Silas sent away by night from Thessalonica to Berea). 'Day after day' renders 'daily'.

Catholic position summarized as scripture and tradition belonging together, guarded by the church's teaching office (magisterium); Orthodox as councils, fathers and the mind of the church. Please check both are fairly put.
'Lutheran and Anglican churches, among others, still say the old creeds' – confirm wording; no count given.
Sola scriptura called 'a watchword of the Protestant Reformation'; the slogan form is later systematization of the Reformers' teaching. Confirm.

Editor pass: hook's invented 'go home' cut (Acts says only that they searched daily); 'the Bible was written inside the church' narrowed to the New Testament (the Old Testament predates the church); 'scripture alone was never meant...' attributed to Protestants rather than said by the narrator.
